entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8271"/><div sID="gen13088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8271"/>3. In speaking of Jesus Christ to others, she regains her own assurance. Literally, "I am for my beloved ... for me." Reverse order from <reference osisRef="Song.2.16">So 2:16</reference>. She now, after the season of darkness, grounds her convictions on His love towards her, more than on hers towards Him (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">De 33:3</reference>). There, it was the young believer concluding that she was His, from the sensible assurance that He was hers. <div eID="gen13088" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8272"/><div sID="gen13089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8272"/><hi type="bold">4. Tirzah--</hi>meaning "pleasant" (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.21">He 13:21</reference>); "well-pleasing" (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">Mt 5:14</reference>); the royal city of one of the old Canaanite kings (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.24">Jos 12:24</reference>); and after the revolt of Israel, the royal city of its kings, before Omri founded Samaria (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.8">1Ki 16:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.15">15</reference>). No ground for assigning a later date than the time of Solomon to the Song, as Tirzah was even in his time the capital of the north (Israel), as Jerusalem was of the south (Judah).<div eID="gen13089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem--</hi>residence of the kings of Judah, as Tirzah, of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.1">Psa 48:1</reference>, &c.; 122:1-3; 125:1, 2). Loveliness, security, unity, and loyalty; also the union of Israel and Judah in the Church (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.13">Is 11:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">Jr 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.16">Eze 37:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22">17, 22</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Re 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen13090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">terrible--</hi>awe-inspiring. Not only armed as a city on the defensive, but as an army on the offensive.<div eID="gen13091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">banners--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.60.4">Psa 60:4</reference>); Jehovah-nissi (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2Co 10:4</reference>). <div eID="gen13092" type="x-p"/>

The "little sister" (<reference osisRef="Song.8.8">So 8:8</reference>) is not inconsistent with her being "the only one"; for that sister is one with herself (<reference osisRef="John.10.16">Joh 10:16</reference>).<div eID="gen13098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">choice--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>). So at her appearance after Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Ac 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.6.15">6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.25">24:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.28">26:28</reference>). <div eID="gen13100" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. Hollow professors, like half wives, have no part in the one bride. only one of her mother-- namely, "Jerusalem above" ( Ga 4:26 ). The "little sister" ( So 8:8 ) is not inconsistent with her being "the only one"; for that sister is one with herself ( Joh 10:16 ). choice-- ( Ep 1:4 ; 2Th 2:13 ). As she exalted Him above all others ( So 5:10 ), so He now her. daughters ... blessed her-- ( Is 8:18 ; 61:9 ; Eze 16:14 ; 2Th 1:10 ). So at her appearance after Pentecost ( Ac 4:13 ; 6:15 ; 24:25 ; 26:28 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8277"/><div sID="gen13101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8277"/>10. The words expressing the admiration of the daughters. Historically (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.24-Acts.5.39">Ac 5:24-39</reference>).<div eID="gen13101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the morning--</hi>As yet she is not come to the fulness of her light (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen13102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">moon--</hi>shining in the night, by light borrowed from the sun; so the bride, in the darkness of this world, reflects the light of the Sun of righteousness (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen13103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sun--</hi>Her light of justification is perfect, for it is His (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.17">1Jo 4:17</reference>). The moon has less light, and has only one half illuminated; so the bride's sanctification is as yet imperfect. Her future glory (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">Mt 13:43</reference>).<div eID="gen13104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">army--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.6.4">So 6:4</reference>). The climax requires this to be applied to the starry and angelic hosts, from which God is called Lord of Sabaoth. Her final glory (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">Ge 15:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.3">Da 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.1">Re 12:1</reference>). The Church Patriarchal, "the morning"; Levitical, "the moon"; Evangelical, "the sun"; Triumphant, "the bannered army" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.14">Re 19:14</reference>). <div eID="gen13105" type="x-p"/>

The moon has less light, and has only one half illuminated; so the bride's sanctification is as yet imperfect. Her future glory ( Mt 13:43 ). army-- ( So 6:4 ). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8278"/><div sID="gen13106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8278"/>11. The bride's words; for she everywhere is the narrator, and often soliloquizes, which He never does. The first garden (<reference osisRef="Song.2.11-Song.2.13">So 2:11-13</reference>) was that of spring, full of flowers and grapes not yet ripe; the second, autumn, with spices (which are always connected with the person of Jesus Christ), and nothing unripe (<reference osisRef="Song.4.13">So 4:13</reference>, &c.). The third here, of "nuts," from the previous autumn; the end of winter, and verge of spring; the Church in the upper room (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.13">Ac 1:13</reference>, &c.), when one dispensation was just closed, the other not yet begun; the hard shell of the old needing to be broken, and its inner sweet kernel extracted [Origen] (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.27">Lu 24:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.32">32</reference>); waiting for the Holy Ghost to usher in spiritual spring. The walnut is meant, with a bitter outer husk, a hard shell, and sweet kernel. So the Word is distasteful to the careless; when awakened, the sinner finds the letter hard, until the Holy Ghost reveals the sweet inner spirit.<div eID="gen13106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruits of the Valley--</hi>Maurer translates, "the blooming products of the river," that is, the plants growing on the margin of the river flowing through the garden. She goes to watch the first sproutings of the various plants. <div eID="gen13107" type="x-p"/>

A willing chariot bore a "willing people"; or Nadib is the Prince, Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>). Entreaty of the daughters of Jerusalem to her, in her chariot-like flight from them (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.12">2Ki 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.14">2Sa 19:14</reference>).<div eID="gen13110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shulamite--</hi>new name applied to her now for the first time. Feminine of Solomon, Prince of Peace; His bride, daughter of peace, accepting and proclaiming it (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Is 52:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.27">Joh 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Ro 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Ep 2:17</reference>). Historically, this name answers to the time when, not without a divine design in it, the young Church met in Solomon's porch (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.11">Ac 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.12">5:12</reference>). The entreaty, "Return, O Shulamite," answers to the people's desire to keep Peter and John, after the lame man was healed, when they were about to enter the temple. Their reply attributing the glory not to themselves, but to Jesus Christ, answers to the bride's reply here, "What will ye see" in me? "As it were," &c. She accepts the name Shulamite, as truly describing her. But adds, that though "one" (<reference osisRef="Song.6.9">So 6:9</reference>), she is nevertheless "two." Her glories are her Lord's, beaming through her (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.31">Ep 5:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.32">32</reference>). The two armies are the family of Jesus Christ in heaven, and that on earth, joined and one with Him; the one militant, the other triumphant. Or Jesus Christ and His ministering angels are one army, the Church the other, both being one (<reference osisRef="John.17.21">Joh 17:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.22">22</reference>). Allusion is made to Mahanaim (meaning two hosts), the scene of Jacob's victorious conflict by prayer (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.2">Ge 32:2</reference>, 9, 22-30). Though she is peace, yet she has warfare here, between flesh and spirit within and foes without; her strength, as Jacob's at Mahanaim, is Jesus Christ and His host enlisted on her side by prayer; whence she obtains those graces which raise the admiration of the daughters of Jerusalem. <chapter eID="Song.6"/>
